title: Space Technology and Satellites
summary: The computing above our heads: how satellites stay in orbit, how GPS pinpoints your location, how Earth observation and AI monitor our planet, how satellite internet works, why space debris is a growing problem, and how to design your own CubeSat mission.
learn: How satellites stay in orbit and the main types of orbit
How satellite navigation works out your position
How Earth observation satellites and AI help monitor the planet
How satellite communication and space internet work
Why space debris is a problem and how it can be managed
How a small satellite mission is designed and the opportunities in the space industry
intro: Every time you check a map, a weather forecast or a live football match, you're using satellites. Thousands of them now circle the Earth, carrying computers, cameras and radios that help us navigate, communicate and protect the planet. In this topic you'll find out how satellites stay up, how GPS works out exactly where you are, how satellite images and AI track floods and wildfires, how space internet reaches remote places, why space junk is a serious threat, and you'll plan a satellite mission of your own.

pages.title: Satellites and orbits
pages.spec: Explain how satellites stay in orbit, compare types of orbit and describe the parts of a satellite
pages.summary: A satellite stays in orbit because it travels sideways fast enough that, as gravity pulls it down, the Earth curves away beneath it. Satellites use different orbits for different jobs: low Earth orbit, medium Earth orbit and geostationary orbit. Every satellite has a power supply, computer, communications and a payload.
pages.starter: If you throw a ball sideways it falls to the ground. What would happen if you could throw it at 28,000 km/h?

LEO (low Earth orbit): 160-2,000 km; ISS, Starlink, imaging satellites

blocks.text: How satellites stay up

A **[[satellite]]** is an object that travels around a larger object. The Moon is a natural satellite; there are now many thousands of artificial ones. An **[[orbit]]** is the curved path a satellite follows. Gravity constantly pulls the satellite towards the Earth, but it moves sideways so quickly (about 28,000 km/h in low orbit) that the Earth curves away beneath it as fast as it falls. It's constantly "falling around" the planet.
Types of orbit

head: Orbit
Height above Earth
Time for one orbit
Used for
rows: International Space Station, Starlink, Earth imaging

blocks.text: A geostationary satellite orbits at the same speed the Earth spins, so it stays above the same point on the equator. That's why satellite TV dishes can point in one fixed direction.
Inside a satellite

blocks.caption: Satellite subsystems
head: Part
Job
rows: Solar panels generate electricity; batteries store it for when the satellite is in Earth's shadow
Controls the satellite, stores data and runs software (which can often be updated from Earth)
Antennas send data to and receive commands from ground stations
Keeps the satellite pointing the right way using small thrusters or spinning wheels
The instruments that do the mission's job: cameras, sensors, radios, telescopes

pages.title: Satellite navigation
pages.spec: Explain how satellite navigation systems work out a receiver's position, and describe their uses and limitations
pages.summary: Satellite navigation (GNSS) uses satellites that broadcast precise time signals from atomic clocks. A receiver measures how long signals take to arrive from at least four satellites, works out its distance from each and calculates its position, a process called trilateration. Timing must be incredibly accurate.
pages.starter: How does your phone know where you are, even when you're not connected to Wi-Fi?
sc: I can describe GNSS systems such as GPS and Galileo
I can explain how trilateration works out a position
I can explain why accurate timing matters and describe limitations

b: GNSS: Global Navigation Satellite System
GPS (USA), Galileo (Europe), GLONASS (Russia), BeiDou (China)
About 24-30 satellites per system, about 20,000 km up
Your phone often uses several systems together
Each satellite broadcasts its position and the exact time
Your receiver measures how long each signal took to arrive
Distance = speed of light × time
With 4 satellites, it calculates your position (trilateration) and corrects its own clock
Radio signals travel at about 300,000 km per second
An error of one millionth of a second = about 300 m wrong
So satellites carry ultra-precise atomic clocks
Banks, power grids and phone networks also rely on GNSS timing

blocks.text: What is GNSS?

A **[[GNSS]]** (Global Navigation Satellite System) is a network of satellites that lets receivers work out their location anywhere on Earth. The best-known is **[[GPS]]**, run by the USA. Europe has Galileo, Russia has GLONASS and China has BeiDou. Most phones use several systems together for better accuracy.
Working out your position

Each satellite broadcasts signals saying where it is and exactly what time the signal was sent, measured by an **[[atomic clock]]**. Your receiver notes when each signal arrives and calculates how far away each satellite is.

blocks.title: Distance from one satellite
blocks.context: A signal travels at about 300,000 km per second and takes 0.07 seconds to arrive.
steps: Distance = speed × time.
blocks.answer: The receiver is about 21,000 km from that satellite, somewhere on a giant sphere around it.

blocks.text: **[[trilateration|Trilateration]]** uses distances from several satellites. One distance puts you somewhere on a sphere around one satellite; two narrow it to a circle; three narrow it to two points (one usually in space); a fourth satellite fixes your position and corrects the small errors in your receiver's own clock.
Why timing matters

Radio signals travel at about 300,000 km per second, so a timing error of just one millionth of a second would put your position about 300 metres out. That's why satellites carry atomic clocks that lose less than a second in millions of years. GNSS timing is also used to synchronise banks, power grids, mobile networks and stock markets.
Limitations

blocks.title: When GNSS struggles
items: Signals are weak and can't pass through buildings or underground
Tall buildings and valleys block or reflect signals ("urban canyons")
Jamming: deliberately blocking signals with radio noise, a growing problem for aircraft and ships in some regions
Spoofing: sending fake signals so a receiver thinks it's somewhere else
Phones combine GNSS with Wi-Fi, mobile masts and motion sensors to fill the gaps

blocks.title: Human GPS
steps: Three pupils stand in the playground or hall as "satellites", each holding a rope or tape measure.
A fourth pupil (the "receiver") is placed secretly. Each satellite measures the distance to the receiver.
On a scale map, draw circles of the right radius around each satellite's position and find where they cross.
Repeat with one measurement deliberately 1 m wrong and see what happens.

q.q: How many circles were needed to find the receiver's position on a flat map, and why?
q.a: Three: one circle gives many possible points, two give two points where they cross, and the third shows which of the two is correct. (In 3D space, with clock errors, four satellites are needed.)

q.q: What happened when one measurement was wrong, and what does this show?
q.a: The circles no longer crossed at one point, so the position was uncertain or wrong. It shows why accurate timing (and therefore distance) is vital.

check.q: What does GNSS stand for?
Which navigation system is run by Europe?
What is the minimum number of satellites a receiver needs for a full position fix?
check.why: Three for position, one for clock correction.

check.q: Why do navigation satellites carry atomic clocks?
o: Tiny timing errors cause big position errors

practice.q: Explain how a GNSS receiver works out its position.
practice.a: Satellites broadcast position and time (1); receiver measures signal travel time to calculate distance (1); uses distances from at least 4 satellites (trilateration) to fix position (1).

practice.q: Give two reasons GNSS may not work well in a city centre or building.
practice.a: Signals blocked by buildings/can't pass through walls (1); reflected signals in urban canyons cause errors (1).

pages.title: Watching the Earth
pages.spec: Describe how Earth observation satellites and AI are used to monitor the planet and respond to disasters
pages.summary: Earth observation satellites use cameras and sensors, including radar that can see through cloud, to monitor weather, climate, farming, floods and wildfires. Programmes such as Copernicus share data freely, and AI helps analyse the enormous number of images. This data supports disaster response and climate science but raises privacy questions.
pages.starter: Name something that is happening on Earth right now that you could spot from space.
sc: I can describe the sensors Earth observation satellites use
I can describe uses of Earth observation data
I can explain how AI helps analyse satellite images

b: Earth observation: studying Earth from space
Optical cameras: like a phone camera, but need daylight and clear skies
Infrared: heat from fires, temperature of the sea
Radar: sees through cloud and works at night
Weather forecasting and climate change: ice, sea level, temperature
Farming: crop health, drought
Disasters: floods, wildfires, earthquakes
Pollution, deforestation, illegal fishing
Satellites send back huge amounts of data every day
AI spots changes: new buildings, flooded fields, burnt forest
Copernicus (EU) data is free for anyone
Privacy: how much should satellites be able to see?

blocks.text: Earth observation
**[[Earth observation]]** means gathering information about the Earth from space. It's a type of **[[remote sensing]]**: measuring something without touching it. Satellites carry different sensors:

blocks.caption: Earth observation sensors
head: Sensor
What it detects
Good for
Limitation
rows: Works through cloud and at night; floods, ice

blocks.text: **[[resolution|Resolution]]** is the size of the smallest detail a satellite image can show. A 10 m resolution image (like many free images) shows fields and large buildings; commercial satellites can show details smaller than 50 cm, enough to see cars.
Uses of Earth observation

blocks.title: How satellite data helps
items: Weather forecasts and storm warnings
Climate science: measuring sea ice, glaciers, sea level and temperature over decades
Farming: spotting crops that need water or fertiliser
Disasters: mapping floods, wildfires and earthquake damage to direct rescue teams
Environment: tracking deforestation, pollution and illegal fishing

blocks.text: **[[Copernicus]]** is the European Union's Earth observation programme. Its Sentinel satellites image the whole planet every few days, and the data is free for anyone to use, including schools. The UK is a member of Copernicus.
AI and satellite data

Earth observation satellites send back many terabytes of data every day: far too much for people to look at. AI models are trained to spot changes automatically, such as newly flooded land, burnt forest, new buildings or ships at sea. This lets emergency services get maps of a disaster within hours.
Privacy and ethics

Very detailed images raise questions: should companies be able to sell images of people's homes? Could satellites be used to track individuals? Rules limit the detail of images sold in some countries, and many argue that the benefits for climate and disaster response outweigh the risks if data is used responsibly.

blocks.title: Disaster response team
steps: Your teacher gives you "before" and "after" satellite images of a flooded area (or use a free online viewer such as Copernicus Browser).
Identify the areas that have flooded and the roads that are cut off.

Write a short briefing for the rescue team: where to go first and why.

q.q: Which sensor would work best on a cloudy day, and why?
q.a: Radar (SAR), because it can see through cloud and works at night, whereas optical cameras can't see the ground through cloud.
E.g. "The main road east of the river is flooded; send boats to the housing estate north of the bridge first, where water has reached homes; use the western road to bring supplies."

pages.title: Space internet and communications
pages.spec: Describe how satellites provide communications and internet access, and evaluate mega-constellations
pages.summary: Communication satellites relay signals between distant places. Traditional internet satellites in geostationary orbit suffer from high latency, so new mega-constellations of thousands of low Earth orbit satellites, such as Starlink, provide faster, lower-latency internet worldwide, even directly to phones. They help connect remote areas but raise concerns about astronomy, debris and control.
pages.starter: How could you get fast internet on a remote island, a ship at sea or a farm on a mountain?
sc: I can explain how communication satellites relay signals
I can explain latency and why LEO satellites reduce it
I can evaluate the benefits and concerns of mega-constellations

b: Communication satellites receive a signal and send it on
Ground stations connect satellites to the internet
Used for TV, phone calls, ships, aircraft and remote areas
Deep space missions talk to Earth through giant dish antennas
Latency: the delay before data arrives
GEO satellites are 35,786 km away: a round trip takes over half a second
LEO satellites are about 550 km away: much lower latency
But LEO satellites move fast, so you need thousands to cover the Earth
Starlink: thousands of satellites, more than half of all active satellites
Other companies and countries are building their own
Satellites can now connect directly to ordinary phones in some places
Concerns: astronomy, debris, and control by a few companies

blocks.text: Communication satellites

A **[[communication satellite]]** receives radio signals from one place on Earth and sends them to another. Signals reach the wider internet through a **[[ground station]]**, a site with large antennas. Satellites carry TV broadcasts and connect ships, aircraft, remote communities and emergency services when ordinary networks are down.
Latency
**[[latency|Latency]]** is the delay between sending data and it arriving. Radio signals travel at the speed of light, but distances in space are huge.

blocks.title: Latency to a geostationary satellite
blocks.context: A geostationary satellite is about 36,000 km above you. Signals travel at 300,000 km/s.
steps: To the satellite and back down to a ground station: 2 × 36,000 = 72,000 km.
Time = 72,000 ÷ 300,000 = 0.24 s, just one way. A reply has to make the same trip back.
blocks.answer: A request and its reply take about half a second or more, which makes video calls and online games feel laggy.

blocks.text: Low Earth orbit satellites are only about 550 km up, so the delay is just a few hundredths of a second. But because they move so fast across the sky, thousands are needed so that one is always overhead.
Mega-constellations

A **[[mega-constellation]]** is a group of hundreds or thousands of satellites working together. SpaceX's Starlink has launched thousands of satellites, more than half of all active satellites in orbit. Other companies and countries are building rival networks, and some satellites can now connect directly to ordinary mobile phones, filling gaps where there's no signal.

blocks.caption: Weighing up mega-constellations
head: Benefits
Concerns
rows: Fast internet for remote and rural areas
Bright satellite trails spoil telescope images and the night sky
Connectivity after disasters and for emergency services
More satellites increase the risk of collisions and debris
Internet for ships, aircraft and remote schools
A few private companies control important infrastructure
Satellites burn up at the end of their lives, with possible effects on the upper atmosphere

blocks.text: Satellite internet has become important in conflicts and disasters, for example keeping communications running in Ukraine. This shows how much power the companies that own these networks can have.

blocks.title: Connect the island
steps: A small island off the coast of Donegal needs internet for its school, a fish farm and holiday cottages.

q.q: Which option do you recommend, and why?
q.a: E.g. LEO satellite: quick to set up, low latency good for video lessons and calls, much cheaper than laying a cable; keep a backup in case of storms.

q.q: Why does the geostationary option have high latency?
q.a: The satellite is about 36,000 km up, so each signal travels about 72,000 km there and back down, and a reply makes the same trip again: around half a second or more in total.

pages.title: Space junk
pages.spec: Explain the causes and dangers of space debris and evaluate ways to make space sustainable
pages.summary: Space debris includes dead satellites, used rocket stages and fragments from collisions and explosions. It travels so fast that even tiny pieces can damage satellites and spacecraft. Too much debris could trigger a chain reaction of collisions. Tracking, avoiding collisions, designing satellites to deorbit and active removal missions all help keep space usable.
pages.starter: A paint fleck hits a window at 28,000 km/h. What damage could it do?
sc: I can describe what space debris is and where it comes from
I can explain why debris is dangerous, including the Kessler syndrome
I can evaluate solutions to the space debris problem

b: Dead satellites and used rocket stages
Fragments from explosions, collisions and anti-satellite tests
Tens of thousands of tracked objects; perhaps over a million pieces larger than 1 cm
At orbital speed, even a paint fleck can crack a window
One collision creates thousands of fragments
Those fragments cause more collisions
A chain reaction could make some orbits unusable for generations
We rely on satellites for navigation, communication and weather
Tracking debris and moving satellites to avoid collisions
Design satellites to deorbit and burn up at the end of their mission
Active debris removal: missions to capture junk (UK companies are leading tests)
International rules and responsible behaviour

blocks.text: What is space debris?

**[[space debris|Space debris]]** (space junk) is any human-made object in orbit that no longer does a useful job: dead satellites, used rocket stages, lost tools and countless fragments from explosions and collisions. Space agencies track tens of thousands of larger objects, and estimate there are over a million pieces bigger than 1 cm.
Why it's dangerous

In low Earth orbit, objects travel at around 28,000 km/h. At that speed, a 1 cm fragment hits with the energy of an exploding hand grenade, and even flecks of paint have chipped windows on the International Space Station. The ISS regularly fires its engines to dodge debris, and satellite operators perform thousands of **[[collision avoidance]]** manoeuvres every year.

The **[[Kessler syndrome]]** is a possible chain reaction: one collision creates thousands of fragments, which hit other satellites, creating more fragments. If it happened, some orbits could become too dangerous to use for many years.

blocks.caption: Major debris events
head: Event
What happened
rows: China destroyed one of its old weather satellites with a missile, creating thousands of pieces of debris
A working US communications satellite and a dead Russian satellite collided, creating thousands of fragments
Russia destroyed an old satellite; ISS astronauts had to shelter in their spacecraft

blocks.text: Making space sustainable

blocks.title: Solutions to space debris
items: Tracking debris with radar and telescopes, and sharing warnings
Collision avoidance: moving satellites out of the way
Designing satellites to **[[deorbit]]** (drop down and burn up) within a few years of their mission ending
Active debris removal: spacecraft that capture junk with magnets, nets or robotic arms
Banning destructive anti-satellite tests

blocks.text: The UK is a leader in space sustainability. ClearSpace and Astroscale, which have UK teams, are developing missions to remove debris, and the UK has pushed for international agreements on responsible behaviour in space.

blocks.title: Junk busters
steps: Read the four debris-removal ideas: magnetic docking, a giant net, a robotic arm, and a laser that nudges junk down.
Score each idea for cost, risk, how many objects it could remove and whether it could be misused.
Choose the best idea, or combine ideas.
Write three "rules of the road" all satellite operators should follow.

q.q: Which idea did you choose, and why?
q.a: E.g. magnetic docking for future satellites (fitted with docking plates) plus robotic arms for old ones; nets could create more fragments and lasers could be misused as weapons.

q.q: Write your three rules of the road.
q.a: E.g. every satellite must deorbit within five years of its mission ending; share orbit data to avoid collisions; no destructive anti-satellite tests.

check.q: What is space debris?
o: Human-made objects in orbit that no longer do a useful job

check.q: Why is small debris dangerous?
o: It travels so fast it hits with huge energy

check.q: What is the Kessler syndrome?
o: A chain reaction of collisions creating more and more debris

check.q: What does it mean to deorbit a satellite?

practice.q: Explain how space debris could make an orbit unusable.
practice.a: One collision creates many fragments (1), which cause further collisions in a chain reaction (Kessler syndrome) (1).

practice.q: Describe three ways to reduce the problem of space debris.
practice.a: Any three: tracking/collision avoidance (1); design satellites to deorbit (1); active removal missions (1); ban anti-satellite tests/international rules (1).

pages.title: Mission design and the space industry
pages.spec: Plan a small satellite mission and describe careers and opportunities in the space industry
pages.summary: CubeSats are small, low-cost satellites built from 10 cm cubes that let universities, schools and start-ups reach space. Designing a mission means choosing a goal, payload, orbit, power, communications and an end-of-life plan. The UK space industry is growing, with jobs in software, data, engineering and science.

blocks.text: CubeSats

A **[[CubeSat]]** is a small satellite built from standard 10 cm cube units, each called 1U. A 3U CubeSat is about the size of a loaf of bread. Because they use standard sizes and off-the-shelf parts, CubeSats are far cheaper than traditional satellites and can share a rocket launch with others. Universities, schools, start-ups and even small countries have launched their own.
Planning a mission

blocks.caption: Mission planning checklist
head: Part
Questions to answer
Example: monitoring Lough Erne water quality
rows: What problem will it solve? Who will use the data?
Detect algae blooms early to protect wildlife and drinking water
Multispectral camera that detects the colour of algae
Low Earth orbit, passing over Ireland regularly
How will data get to Earth?
Radio downlink to a ground station
Who controls it and processes data?
Ground station plus software and AI to produce maps
Low orbit so it burns up within 5 years

blocks.text: The space industry

The space industry is one of the UK's fast-growing high-tech sectors. Glasgow builds more small satellites than almost anywhere outside the United States, and the UK has developed **[[spaceport|spaceports]]**, such as SaxaVord in Shetland, to launch small rockets from UK soil. Most space jobs aren't astronauts: they're in software, data science, engineering, manufacturing, law, business and communications. Many companies use satellite data in farming, insurance, shipping and climate services.

blocks.title: Space careers
items: Software engineer: writing code for satellites and ground systems
Data scientist: turning satellite data into useful information
Systems engineer: making all the parts of a mission work together
Space lawyer or policy adviser: rules, licences and debris
Mission operator: controlling satellites from the ground

blocks.text: The UK Space Agency and ESA run education programmes and competitions for schools, and some schools have had experiments flown in space. Ask your teacher about current opportunities.

q.q: Complete your mission plan: objective, payload and orbit.
q.a: E.g. "PeatWatch": objective: monitor the health and wetness of Fermanagh's peatlands to protect carbon stores; payload: multispectral and thermal camera; orbit: LEO, sun-synchronous so images are taken at the same time of day.

q.q: How will your CubeSat avoid becoming space junk?
q.a: Use a low orbit so atmospheric drag brings it down within 5 years, or fit a drag sail that opens at the end of the mission to speed up reentry.
